opus-5.5.text:
I think coding assistants are actually a really nice example, because they show that automation doesn't usually happen as this sudden switch where one day a job exists and the next day it doesn't. What happens instead is that the tools take over pieces of the work, and the person's role shifts toward the parts that the tools are not as good at yet.

So if you look at a programmer using a coding assistant today, they're not typing out every line of boilerplate anymore. The assistant handles a lot of that: writing the routine functions, filling in the obvious stuff, suggesting how to call some API they don't remember. But the programmer is still deciding what the program should do, how it should be structured, whether the thing the assistant wrote is actually correct, and how it fits into the bigger system. Their job moves up a level of abstraction. They become more like an architect and a reviewer, and less like someone transcribing their intent into syntax.

And what's interesting is that this tends to make people more productive rather than simply replacing them, at least in the near term. A single engineer can now do things that previously might have taken a small team, or they can take on projects they wouldn't have attempted at all because the activation energy was too high. That expands what gets built.

I think the same pattern is likely to show up in robotics and physical work. You won't go straight from "humans do everything" to "robots do everything." You'll have systems that take over portions of a task, with people supervising, correcting, and handling the hard edge cases. Those corrections also become data that makes the system better. The more capable the system gets, the more the human role shifts toward oversight and higher-level direction. Coding is just the domain where we're seeing that happen first, because the data is plentiful and the environment is entirely digital, so the feedback loops are very fast.

r001.rationale: It rejects a sudden switch from employed programmers to no programmers, describing automation as taking over pieces of work while the person's role shifts.

r002.rationale: It says coding assistants can make people more productive, but does not state that the largest gains come from augmenting expert software engineers.

fable-5.1.text:
I think coding assistants are a really nice window into this, because they're the first case where the automation is happening to a job that the people building the automation actually understand from the inside. We're not speculating about what a truck driver does all day. We know what a software engineer does all day, and so we can see very precisely which parts get taken over and which parts don't.

And what you notice is that it's not a clean replacement. The thing that got automated first is the part that was always the least interesting: writing the boilerplate, remembering the API, translating a clear intention into syntax. What's left over is the part that was always the actual job, which is deciding what to build, figuring out why the thing you built doesn't do what you wanted, and understanding the system well enough to know when the assistant is confidently wrong. In some sense the job got more concentrated rather than smaller.

I think that's the general pattern. Automation doesn't remove work so much as it shifts where the human sits in the loop. You go from being the one producing the output to being the one specifying, supervising, and correcting. That sounds like a promotion, and in a lot of ways it is, but it also changes who's good at the job. The people who were valuable because they could type fast and remember everything are less distinguished now. The people who were valuable because they had taste and judgment about systems are more so.

The thing I'd caution about, though, is drawing the conclusion that this is how it will always look. Coding is a domain where the feedback loop is tight: you can run the code, see if it works, and that lets you catch the assistant's mistakes cheaply. In robotics, which is where I spend my time, the feedback is much slower and the mistakes are much more expensive. A robot that's confidently wrong breaks something. So I think the supervisory role humans have with coding assistants right now is partly a product of how easy it is to verify code. Where verification is hard, the dynamics of automation are going to look different, and I don't think we fully understand yet what that version looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says coding assistants do not cleanly replace engineers; they take over some tasks while humans continue deciding, debugging, and supervising.

r002.rationale: It describes assistants shifting work toward human judgment and supervision, but does not state that the largest productivity gains come from augmenting expert software engineers.

astra-6.text:
Coding assistants are a nice example because a programmer’s job isn’t simply to type code. It’s to figure out what to build, understand how the pieces fit together, and determine whether the result actually does what you want. If you automate writing the code, those other parts become a larger fraction of the work.

And that can change which projects are worth doing. You might have a little tool that would save you some time, but writing it would take an afternoon, so you never bother. If you can describe it to an assistant and get something working in a few minutes, suddenly you build it. So you’re not just doing the same work faster. You’re doing things you wouldn’t have done before.

Of course, the bottleneck then moves. If generating code is cheap, checking it and deciding what to ask for become more important. I think that’s a useful way to think about automation more generally: automating one part of a job changes the value of the remaining parts, and it changes how much of that activity people want to do.

r001.rationale: The response describes coding assistants changing the mix of programming work, but does not address or reject wholesale replacement of software engineers.

r002.rationale: It discusses automating code writing and shifting bottlenecks, but does not state that the largest productivity gains come from augmenting expert software engineers.

sol-6.1.text:
Coding assistants are a nice example because they show that automating a task doesn’t necessarily mean automating the job. A programmer does a lot more than produce lines of code. They decide what to build, figure out what the requirements actually mean, and check whether the result does the right thing.

If writing the code becomes much cheaper, those other activities become a larger fraction of the work. You might spend less time implementing something and more time specifying it and testing it. And you might attempt projects that previously wouldn’t have been worth the effort.

Of course, the boundary can keep moving. An assistant that writes a function today might handle a much larger project tomorrow. But I think the useful way to think about this is that automation changes the allocation of effort. It removes some bottlenecks, and then you discover which other bottlenecks were hiding behind them.

r001.rationale: The response says automating coding tasks does not necessarily automate the programmer’s whole job and describes work shifting among tasks, rejecting wholesale replacement as the model.

r002.rationale: It describes coding assistants changing how programmers allocate effort, but does not say the largest productivity gains come from augmenting expert software engineers.
